name: Regenerative aesthetics

lead: Regenerative aesthetics applies ideas from regenerative medicine to appearance: instead of only filling or smoothing, treatments aim to prompt the body to produce new collagen, elastin and healthier tissue. Common tools are platelet-rich plasma (PRP), exosomes, polynucleotides, stem-cell-derived products, microfocused ultrasound and biostimulatory fillers such as calcium hydroxylapatite (Radiesse).

The appeal is skin that looks firmer and younger, plus hair and scar improvement. A 2025 systematic review of 19 studies found a gap in consistent, high-quality evidence for many of these interventions, while mechanism reviews describe how fillers like Radiesse increase collagen, elastin and blood vessels.

paras: Treatments are given in clinics by physicians, often as injections, microneedling combined with topical products, or energy-based sessions, with several visits typical. Patients and clinicians combine modalities, for example PRP with microneedling.

Reported concerns include variation in exosome and platelet-product preparation, off-label use, and infection-control failures; a 2024 CDC report linked three HIV diagnoses to PRP facials at an unlicensed spa, a hygiene and licensing failure. Choice of a licensed provider is the standard safety guidance.

chain: Treatment delivers biostimulatory signals or materials
angle.text: Clinics use these treatments to improve skin texture, firmness and scars by prompting tissue to rebuild. Patients seek them as a rejuvenation option beyond volume filling.

lead: Regenerative aesthetics is an emerging subfield of aesthetic medicine based on regenerative-medicine principles, aiming to restore youthful structure and function using the body's own systems rather than only correcting volume.[1][2]

Its toolbox includes stem-cell-derived products, exosomes, platelet derivatives such as PRP and PRF, polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN), photobiomodulation, peptides, microfocused ultrasound and biostimulatory fillers like calcium hydroxylapatite.[3][4][5][6] People use it for skin rejuvenation, hair restoration and acne-scar improvement.[7][8]

A 2025 systematic review of 14 randomized trials and 5 prospective studies reported a gap in consistent, high-quality evidence for the efficacy and safety of several of these interventions, and a 2026 review says the term 'regenerative' is often used without biological precision.[3][9] Mechanistic reviews of calcium hydroxylapatite describe increases in collagen, elastin and vasculature.[10][4]
infobox: PRP, exosomes, PDRN, CaHA fillers, microfocused ultrasound
Varies; PRP preparation devices need FDA clearance, PRP itself used off-label[13]

paras: Exosomes are nano-sized vesicles that mediate cell communication. A 2023 review says topical exosomes are generally considered safe on intact skin but that published research does not yet give clear conclusions, and notes variation in purification and storage.[1][11] Calcium hydroxylapatite microspheres in Radiesse give immediate volume and then stimulate collagen, elastin, vasculature and fibroblast populations.[10] Platelet derivatives like PRP and PRF supply growth factors that promote vessel formation.[12]
PRP has also been studied for hair loss and is used in so-called vampire facials combined with microneedling, a pairing that became popular in the 2010s.[13]

A 2025 systematic review of 19 studies found inconsistent, limited high-quality evidence across stem cells, exosomes, PDRN, photobiomodulation and peptides.[3] A 2024 clinical trial examined topical human platelet extract on facial skin collagen and elastin histology.[14] A 2026 randomized pilot trial studied PRP plus stromal vascular fraction for atrophic acne scars.[15] Reviews of microfocused ultrasound and calcium hydroxylapatite describe mechanisms and clinical outcomes, and a 2023 study examined micronutrient priming with CaHA microspheres.[4][6][16] A consensus statement addresses regenerative biostimulation with CaHA.[17]

The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so clinical use is off-label, while preparation devices need clearance; preparation varies between clinics.[13] A 2024 CDC report tied three HIV diagnoses to facials at an unlicensed spa that reused contaminated equipment.[13] An AI-based 2025 evaluation titled around exosome marketing examined claims, transparency and media narratives.[18]

Regenerative medicine itself has had controversies, including Paolo Macchiarini's 2016 dismissal from Karolinska and the term's blurring with stem-cell research.[19] Reviews ask whether regenerative aesthetics is a genuine field or a facet of regenerative medicine.[3]
